chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Utba, from Isma'il ibn 'Ammar, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him: 'I have relatives upon whom I spend, and I prefer some of them over others. When the time for zakat comes, should I give them from it?' He said: 'Are they worthy of it?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'They are better than others, give them.' I said: 'Then who among my relatives am I obliged to support such that I do not count the zakat as a discharge of duty towards them?' He said: 'Your father and your mother.' I said: 'Your father and your mother?' He said: 'The parents and the children.'

key_terms.أَحْتَسِب: To count/consider as discharge of duty

ai.seo_question: Who are the relatives for whom giving zakat counts as fulfilling the obligation of maintenance?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between voluntary charity (sadaqah) and obligatory maintenance (nafaqah) within the family unit, a key topic in Shia fiqh. It establishes that while worthy relatives may receive zakat, such payments do not discharge the giver's mandatory financial duty (nafaqah) except in the specific case of parents and children, where the two obligations merge. This ruling underscores the hierarchical priority of immediate lineage in Islamic inheritance and support structures.
